workEn: Popol Vuh (The Council Book of the K'iche' Maya)
title: Are chic xchi ca ꜩihoh calaxic
titleEn: Popol Vuh — The birth of Hunahpu and Xbalanque; their elder brothers become monkeys
part: The birth of Hunahpu and Xbalanque; their elder brothers become monkeys
source: Popol Vuh, “The birth of Hunahpu and Xbalanque; their elder brothers become monkeys”, from the only surviving copy: the K'iche' text in the hand of Fray Francisco Ximénez, written at Chichicastenango c. 1701–1703 (Newberry Library, Chicago, Ayer MS 1515, fols. 18r–19r, left-hand column), read from the Library of Congress / World Digital Library images; public domain. The text is the manuscript's own spelling, including the colonial letters ꜩ (tz), ꜯ (tz'), ꜭ (k'), ꜭh (ch') and ꜫ (q'), v for u and w, z for s, h for j, and c/qu for both k and q. Where Ximénez's cursive makes these letters hard to tell apart, the reading of Brasseur de Bourbourg's edition (Paris, 1861), made from the same manuscript, was used as a check. Word division, punctuation, capitals and quotation marks are editorial. The ꜩ→tz button shows every word in the modern K'iche' alphabet; there an ejective or glottal stop the scribe left unmarked is supplied where the word is certain, and a word whose modern form is uncertain is simply respelled. Pronunciation: modern K'iche' values for the modern spelling, an admitted convention. No prepared audio yet. All translations were made fresh from the K'iche' for Lectorium.

sentences.t: Are chic xchi ca ꜩihoh calaxic Hunahpu, Xbalanque.
sentences.l: This now shall we-tell their-being-born Hunahpu, Xbalanque.
sentences.i: Now we shall tell of the birth of Hunahpu and Xbalanque.
sentences.n: Ximénez's indented heading, announced at the end of the last part. xchi ca ꜩihoh 'we shall tell': xchi-, the future, written apart, + ca- 'we' + ꜩihoh 'tell' (ꜩih 'word' + -oh). calaxic 'their being born': c- (qui- 'their' before a vowel) + al 'child' + -ax, the passive, + -ic (toggle kalaxik).

sentences.t: Arecut calaxic vae xchi ca biyh. Ta xuric vꜫih calaxic, ta xalan puch ri capoh Xquic vbi.
sentences.l: This-then their-being-born this shall we-tell. When it-reached its-day their-being-born, when she-gave-birth also the maiden Xquic her-name.
sentences.i: This, then, is the birth we shall tell. When the day of their birth came, the maiden called Xquic gave birth.
sentences.n: Ximénez indents this line too: a second heading, then the story. biyh 'tell' as printed since 008 (the manuscript has a mark over the y). Ta xuric 'when it reached' is one word in the manuscript (taxuric), divided with Brasseur's ta x-u riq: x- (completed action) + v- 'it' + ric 'find, reach' (toggle xuriq). vꜫih calaxic 'the day of their birth': v- 'its' + ꜫih 'day'; the manuscript has vquih, the q-shaped letter + u read as the tresillo with Brasseur's u gih. xalan 'she gave birth': al 'child' + -an, which makes a verb (inferred), the root of calaxic. capoh 'maiden' (toggle q'apoj).

sentences.t: Macu xu vachih atit ta xe alaxic; libah chi xe yaqueic e caib chi calaxic, Hunahpu, Xbalanque qui bi; pa huiub xe yaque vi.
sentences.l: Not-then she-faced(?) grandmother when they were-born; instantly (chi) they came-forth(?) they two in their-being-born, Hunahpu, Xbalanque their-name; on mountain they came-forth(?) there.
sentences.i: But the grandmother was not there to see them born; all at once the two came forth (?) at their birth, Hunahpu and Xbalanque by name; it was on the mountain that they came forth.
sentences.n: Macu 'but not': ma 'not' + cu 'then', written as one word (toggle Mak'u). xu vachih 'she faced it': vach 'face' + -ih; in an earlier part the same word was guessed as 'effort', but here Brasseur has 'La vieille n'assista pas', and 'was there to see' is inferred. xe alaxic 'they were born': al + passive -ax + -ic. libah chi 'instantly'. xe yaqueic, xe yaque vi: the yaqueic of 009 and 013 (both guesses there), here plainly the birth itself, 'came forth', after Brasseur's 'ils se produisirent' (inferred; toggle yakeik, yake). e caib 'the two of them'. huiub 'mountain' is written so here and in ¶4, huyub in ¶21; both are printed as written, and the toggle gives juyub' for both. vi points back to pa huiub: 'on the mountain, there'.

sentences.t: Ta xe oc cut pa ha; macu que varic. “He a ꜩaca vloc; quiꜩih chach qui chi,” xꜭha ri atit.
sentences.l: Then they entered then in house; not-then they sleep. “Go you throw-them(?) hither; truly chach(?) their mouth,” she-said the grandmother.
sentences.i: Then they went into the house, but they would not sleep. “Go, throw them out (?); truly their mouths are loud (?),” said the grandmother.
sentences.n: xe oc pa ha 'they went into the house' (oc 'enter', toggle ok; ha 'house', toggle ja): the babies are taken in. que varic 'they sleep': c- (ongoing) + e 'they' + var 'sleep' + -ic, the var of vvarabal 'its sleeping place'. He a ꜩaca vloc: he is taken as the 'go' of 010 (he, ho, hix), here a command (inferred); a 'you (one)'; ꜩaca 'throw down, cast away' is a guess from Brasseur's 'Va les jeter dehors' and the tzaq 'fall' of the modern language (the tz ligature with its ascender is clear at 2.2×; toggle tzaqa). chach is not otherwise known; 'loud' is a guess from Brasseur's 'en vérité ils ne font que crier'. qui chi 'their mouths' (chi 'mouth', toggle chi'): the manuscript has a raised t-like mark over chi, taken as Ximénez's heavy accent, as 013's huvi. quiꜩih 'truly'.

sentences.t: Catecut ta xe ya pa zanic; quz cu qui varam chiri. Xe el chicu chiri, xe ya chic chuvi quix.
sentences.l: Then-then when they were-put on ants; sweet then their sleep there. They went-out then there, they were-put again on-top thorns.
sentences.i: So they were put on an anthill, and there their sleep was sweet. They came away from there, and were put on thorns.
sentences.n: xe ya 'they were put': ya 'give, put' with xe 'they' and no person for the doer, taken as passive in sense, as Brasseur's 'on les porta' (inferred). pa zanic 'on the ants', an anthill: zanic 'ants' (MS pazanic, divided; Brasseur prints pu zanic, the manuscript has a). quz 'sweet, pleasant' is written with a q-shaped letter + u where Brasseur has guz; kept as written, as 012's quz (toggle kus); Brasseur 'leur sommeil y fut savoureux'. qui varam 'their sleep': var + -am. Xe el 'they went out', taken from the anthill; chicu is chic + cu (MS chicu; Brasseur chi cu). chuvi quix 'on top of thorns': chuvi 'on top of' (chi + v- 'its' + vi 'head'); quix 'thorn' (Brasseur qix, his q for ꜭ; toggle k'ix, the known word), not the quix 'you (pl.)' of earlier parts.

sentences.t: Are ta cut xcah Hunbaꜩ, Hunchouen, xe cam ta chiri pa zanic, xe cam ta pu chuvi quix; xcah rumal qui chaquimal, qui ꜫaꜫvachibal puch cumal Hunbaꜩ, Hunchouen.
sentences.l: This (ta) then they-wanted Hunbaꜩ, Hunchouen, they die (ta) there on ants, they die (ta) also on-top thorns; they-wanted-it because their rivalry(?), their envy also by-them Hunbaꜩ, Hunchouen.
sentences.i: This is what Hunbatz and Hunchouen wanted: that they should die there on the anthill, that they should die on the thorns. They wanted it out of rivalry (?) and envy, Hunbatz and Hunchouen did.
sentences.n: xcah 'they wanted': x- + c- 'they' (qui- before a vowel) + ah 'want', as in rah 'he wants' (Brasseur x-c'ah; toggle xkaj); the same letters are xcah 'it went down' in ¶7 (Brasseur x-kah). xe cam ta … xe cam ta pu 'that they die … that they die too', a couplet, with ta of wishing. qui chaquimal, qui ꜫaꜫvachibal puch is a couplet: chaquimal is not otherwise known, and 'rivalry' is Brasseur's ('ils étaient leurs rivaux'), a guess; ꜫaꜫvachibal 'envy' follows Brasseur's cakvachibal: ꜫaꜫ 'fire, red' + vach 'face' + -ibal, perhaps a burning face (inferred). Both letters of ꜫaꜫ are clear 3-shaped tresillos at 2.2× (as 012's ꜫaꜫ, where Brasseur also has cak); the toggle respells the letters (q'aq'wachib'al). In Hunchouen the manuscript has hunchoven here; it is printed u, as in 009–013.

sentences.t: Maui xe culax pa ha cumal qui chac nabec; xa maui quetaam, xavi cu pa huiub xe quiy vi.
sentences.l: Not they were-received in house by-them, their younger-brothers, first; only not they-knew-them, so then on mountain they grew(?) there.
sentences.i: From the first their younger brothers were not taken into the house by them; they simply would not know them, and so it was on the mountain that they grew up (?).
sentences.n: xe culax 'they were received': cul 'meet, receive' (as culvachih 'meet face to face' in ¶22) + passive -ax (inferred; toggle kulax); cumal 'by them', the elder brothers. Read straight on, cumal qui chac would be 'by their younger brothers', which the story cannot mean; cumal is taken as complete in itself ('by them'), and qui chac 'their younger brothers' as naming who was not received, set after the verb phrase, as Brasseur reads it ('leurs jeunes frères ne furent pas reçus par eux dans la maison'; inferred). qui chac 'their younger brothers': chac with plain c (Brasseur chag, his g for ꜫ; toggle chaq', as 011's vchac). quetaam 'they knew them': qu- (qui- before a vowel) + etaam 'know', here in the sense of owning them as kin (inferred). xe quiy vi is a doubtful reading: the manuscript has xequiy vi, the y with a descender and two dots at 2.2×, where Brasseur prints x-e quim vi; it is printed as written and taken as ꜭiy 'grow, multiply' (modern k'iy) with the plain qu Ximénez often writes for k', after Brasseur's 'ils furent élevés dans la montagne' (inferred). Since the reading is doubtful the toggle respells the letters (kiy).

sentences.t: E cu nimac ahzu, ahbix ri Hunbaꜩ, Hunchouen. Xe nimaquir cut nima caxcol rail; xe icou vi, xe caxcobizaxic; e nimac etamanel chic xe uxic.
sentences.l: They then great flute-players, singers the Hunbaꜩ, Hunchouen. They grew-up then great suffering rail(?); they passed there, they were-made-to-suffer; they great knowers now they-became.
sentences.i: Now Hunbatz and Hunchouen were great flute players and singers. They had grown up in great suffering and hardship (?); they had passed through it, they had been made to suffer, and they had become great sages.
sentences.n: ahzu, ahbix 'flute player, singer': ah- 'one who' + zu 'flute', bix 'song', the crafts of 009. Before ahzu a heavy blot covers one letter, which is not printed. Xe nimaquir 'they grew up': nimac 'great' + -ir, 'become' (the r small and raised in the manuscript). caxcol 'suffering' (Brasseur qaxcol, his q for ꜭ; toggle k'axk'ol, the known word). rail is not otherwise known (MS raíl, an accent on the i; Brasseur rail); 'hardship' is a guess from his 'grands travaux', and the toggle respells the letters. xe icou vi 'they passed through it' (icou 'pass'). xe caxcobizaxic 'they were made to suffer': caxcol made a verb with the causative -obiz, then passive -ax + -ic (inferred; toggle k'axk'ob'isaxik). e nimac etamanel 'great sages': etamanel 'one who knows', as in the first part. xe uxic 'they became' (ux 'become').

sentences.t: Xavi xere e ahzu, e ahbix, e pu ahzibab, ahcot xe uxic; ronohel chuꜩin cumal.
sentences.l: Just so they flute-players, they singers, they also painters, carvers they-became; all it-is-completed by-them.
sentences.i: So they became flute players and singers, painters and carvers too; everything they made came out perfect.
sentences.n: The list again, the names but the last with e, the plural 'they are' (ahcot has none): ahzibab 'painter, writer' is ꜩib 'paint, write' (009's ahꜩibenai) + -ab, with Ximénez's plain z (the stroke above is the h's ascender; Brasseur ahtzibab); as 012's vzibel and 013's zibanic the toggle respells the letter (ajsib'ab'). ahcot 'carver' (MS ah cot, written apart, joined as ahzu, ahbix, ahzibab; toggle ajkot as in 009). chuꜩin 'it is complete, finished' (inferred; Brasseur 'tout sortait parfait de leurs mains').

sentences.t: Xa xquetaam vi xe alaxic, xa xe nauinac e pu vꜫexel qui cahau ri xebe chi Xibalba, caminac vi qui cahau.
sentences.l: Only they-knew-it there they were-born, only they had-come-to-know they also replacement their fathers the they-went to Xibalba, dead there their fathers.
sentences.i: They knew well that the twins had been born; they had come to know that these were the replacement of their fathers, who had gone to Xibalba, where their fathers had died.
sentences.n: xquetaam 'they knew it': x- + qu- 'they' + etaam 'know'. xe nauinac 'they had come to know': nao 'know' + -inac, the state reached (013's nauinac 'wise'). e pu vꜫexel qui cahau 'they too were the replacement of their fathers': vꜫexel 'its replacement, in exchange', the house rendering (MS vquexel, the q-shaped letter + u read ꜫ with Brasseur's gexel; toggle uq'exel). The knowers are Hunbatz and Hunchouen; that the replacements are the twins is how Brasseur reads it ('ils étaient les représentants de leurs pères') and fits the story (inferred). qui cahau 'their fathers', Hunhunahpu and Vucub Hunahpu, who went to Xibalba in 010 and died in 011; caminac 'dead' (cam 'die' + -inac).

sentences.t: E cu nimac etamanel ri Hunbaꜩ, Hunchouen; chi qui ꜭux ronohel nabec quetaam ta xe vinaquir ri qui chac.
sentences.l: They then great knowers the Hunbaꜩ, Hunchouen; in their heart all first they-knew-it when they came-into-being the their younger-brothers.
sentences.i: For Hunbatz and Hunchouen were great sages: in their hearts they had known everything from the first, when their younger brothers came into being.
sentences.n: chi qui ꜭux 'in their heart': the manuscript writes qux with the q-shaped letter, read ꜭ as in 009. nabec 'at first'. xe vinaquir 'they came into being': vinac 'person' + -ir, the verb of vinaquirem 'creation' in the first part. qui chac 'their younger brothers' (toggle chaq').

sentences.t: Macu xel apanoc qui nauiquil rumal qui ꜫaꜫvachibal; xa chiquih xcah vi vyoc qui ꜭux; maui banoh xe poizaxic cumal ri Hunahpu, Xbalanque.
sentences.l: Not-then it-went-out thither their wisdom because their envy; only behind-them it-fell there its-ill-will(?) their heart; not deed they were-poizaxic(?) by-them the Hunahpu, Xbalanque.
sentences.i: But their wisdom did not show itself, because of their envy; the ill will (?) of their hearts fell back upon themselves, though no deed of Hunahpu and Xbalanque had given them offence (?).
sentences.n: Macu xel apanoc 'it did not come out': xel 'it went out', apanoc 'thither, away'. qui nauiquil 'their wisdom' (nao 'know'). qui ꜫaꜫvachibal 'their envy', as in ¶4. xa chiquih 'only behind them, upon themselves' (chi + qu- + ih 'back'). xcah vi: the manuscript has xcahvi with a raised accent over vi, clear at 3.5×; xcah here is 'it went down, fell' (Brasseur x-kah; toggle xqaj), not the xcah 'they wanted' of ¶4. vyoc (MS v yoc, joined as vbi; Brasseur u yog) was guessed in 009 as 'what wounds'; here 'ill will' follows Brasseur's 'le mauvais vouloir de leur cœur' (a guess). maui banoh 'no deed'. xe poizaxic is not otherwise known; 'given offence' follows Brasseur's 'quoique aucun acte ne les eût provoqués' (a guess; toggle by the letters).

sentences.t: Xa cu vvbanic chi qui bano hutaꜫih; maui que loꜫoxic rumal ri ratit, Hunbaꜩ, Hunchouen;
sentences.l: Only then blowgunning (chi) they do-it each-day; not they are-loved by the his-grandmother(?), Hunbaꜩ, Hunchouen;
sentences.i: All they did, day after day, was hunt with the blowgun; they were not loved by the grandmother, nor by Hunbatz and Hunchouen;
sentences.n: vvbanic 'blowgunning', the noun of 008's vvbah 'shoot with the blowgun' (written across the page turn, xacu- | vvbanic; Brasseur u ubanic; toggle wub'anik). hutaꜫih 'every day' (MS hutaquih, as 007 and 013). que loꜫoxic 'they are loved': c- + e 'they' + loꜫ 'love, hold dear' + passive -ox + -ic (MS a 3-shaped tresillo; Brasseur logoxic; toggle loq'oxik, the modern loq'). rumal ri ratit is a doubtful reading: the first letter of ratit is an i-like stroke with a hook, taken as Ximénez's r with Brasseur's r'atit; it may be ri atit with a stray stroke. r- 'his, her' + atit 'grandmother' could also make 'the grandmother of Hunbatz and Hunchouen', the owner named after the noun as in 013's vchuch Hunbaꜩ; the English follows Brasseur's 'ni de leur aïeule, ni de Hunbatz, ni de Hunchouen'.

sentences.t: maui chi ia qui va; xhaninac vaim, xe pu vainac ri Hunbaꜩ, Hunchouen, ta que vlic.
sentences.l: not (chi) given their food; finished(?) eating, they also had-eaten the Hunbaꜩ, Hunchouen, when they arrive-here.
sentences.i: they were given no food: only when the meal was over (?), when Hunbatz and Hunchouen had eaten, did they come in.
sentences.n: maui chi ia qui va 'their food was not given': ia is ya 'give' with i for y (Brasseur ya), with no doer named, as xe ya in ¶3; chi stands for chic; va 'food' (toggle wa). xhaninac vaim is a doubtful reading: the letter after x has a closed loop like a b, read h with Brasseur's x-haninak; 'finished' is his sense ('seulement quand le repas était terminé'), a guess, and the toggle respells the letters. vaim 'the meal' (va + -im) and vainac 'having eaten' (va + -inac, the state reached, like caminac 'dead') are inferred. que vlic 'they come in' (vl 'arrive here' + -ic).

sentences.t: Macu que cacaric, oiouaric; xa chi qui cuya. Xere quetaam ri qui ꜭoheic, queheri zac ca quilo.
sentences.l: Not-then they angered(?), raged; only (chi) they endured-it. So they-knew the their being, like light they see-it.
sentences.i: But they did not grow angry or rage; they simply bore it. They knew their own nature, and saw it as clear as day.
sentences.n: que cacaric, oiouaric 'they grow angry, they rage', a couplet: cacar is 013's cacal 'angry' (a guess there; xcacar again in ¶10); oiouaric (MS oio-|uaric; Brasseur oyovaric) is oyoual 'anger' (modern oyowal) made a verb (toggle oyowarik). qui cuya 'they bore it, endured it' (inferred; Brasseur 'se contentant de souffrir'). qui ꜭoheic 'their being, their nature' (MS g-shaped; Brasseur qoheic), the word of the first part. queheri zac 'like the light', that is, plainly. ca quilo 'they see it': the ongoing c- with its vowel, written apart, + qu- 'they' (qui- before a vowel) + il 'see' + -o (toggle kilo; the same letters are qilo 'we see it' in ¶18).

sentences.t: Cucaam cut qui ꜯiquin ta que vlic hutaꜫih; chi qui ti cut ri Hunbaꜩ, Hunchouen; mahabi naquila chi ia chiquech, qui cabichal ri Hunahpu, Xbalanque.
sentences.l: They-carry then their birds when they arrive-here each-day; (chi) they eat-them then the Hunbaꜩ, Hunchouen; not-there-is anything (chi) given to-them, the-two-of-them the Hunahpu, Xbalanque.
sentences.i: So they would bring in their birds when they came each day, and Hunbatz and Hunchouen would eat them; nothing was given to either of them, Hunahpu or Xbalanque.
sentences.n: Cucaam 'they carry (it)': c-, the ongoing, + v- 'he, it' + caam 'carried', the word 013 read in Xquic's va vcaam; the singular v- with two carriers is as 012's cucaam (inferred; Brasseur c'a caam). The toggle gives kukaam by the letters, as 012 gave this same form; 005 and 013 restored the ejective in vcaam (uk'aam), and the 'take' verb is still unsettled, so nothing is restored here. ꜯiquin 'bird'. chi qui ti 'they eat them': ti 'eat (flesh)' (inferred, with Brasseur's 'les mangeaient'; toggle by the letters). mahabi naquila 'nothing at all'. qui cabichal 'the two of them', as 008's vcabichal 'together' (Brasseur 'à l'un ou à l'autre').

sentences.t: Xa cu zu, xa pu bix chi qui bano Hunbaꜩ, Hunchouen.
sentences.l: Only then flute, only also song (chi) they do-it Hunbaꜩ, Hunchouen.
sentences.i: Hunbatz and Hunchouen did nothing but play the flute and sing.
sentences.n: xa zu, xa pu bix 'only flute, only song', the couplet of 013 (xa zu, xa bix ca qui bano), set here against the twins' xa cu vvbanic of ¶8: the elder brothers play, the younger hunt.

sentences.t: Ta xe vl chi puch ri Hunahpu, Xbalanque, mahabi chic qui ꜯiquin cucaam; xe oc vloc, xcacar curi atit.
sentences.l: When they arrived-here (chi) also the Hunahpu, Xbalanque, not-there-is now their birds they-carry; they entered hither, she-was-angry then-the grandmother.
sentences.i: Then Hunahpu and Xbalanque came home, carrying no birds this time; they came in, and the grandmother was angry.
sentences.n: xe vl 'they came here' (vl 'arrive here'). mahabi chic 'none now'. xe oc vloc 'they came in'. xcacar 'she grew angry', the cacar of ¶9 (MS xcacarcuri; Brasseur x-cakar; toggle xkakar by the letters). curi 'then' (cu + ri).

sentences.t: “Naquipa rumal mahabi chi ꜯiquin iucaam?” xe vꜭhax cut ri Hunahpu, Xbalanque.
sentences.l: “What because not-there-is (chi) birds you-carry?” they-were-told then the Hunahpu, Xbalanque.
sentences.i: “Why have you brought no birds?” Hunahpu and Xbalanque were asked.
sentences.n: Naquipa rumal 'why': naquipa 'what' + rumal 'because'. iucaam 'you carry' is a doubtful form: the manuscript has iucaam, u not v (Brasseur yv caam); i- 'you (pl.)' is joined, as 004's ivumal, and the letters are printed as written (as 004's iuecha). It is taken as i- + vcaam, as Cucaam in ¶9 (toggle iukaam, by the letters). xe vꜭhax 'they were told': the passive of ꜭha 'say', with xe 'they' (MS xevghax).

sentences.t: “Are vi, ix catit: xa mi xe tanatob ca ꜯiquin chuvi che,” xꜭha cut.
sentences.l: “This there, you our-grandmother: only just-now they got-stuck(?) our birds on-top tree,” he-said then.
sentences.i: “This is why, grandmother: our birds have got caught (?) up in the tree,” said one of them.
sentences.n: Are vi 'this is why', vi pointing back to the question. ix catit 'you, our grandmother': ix is the plural 'you', of respect, and catit is ca- 'our' + atit (toggle qatit, as in 002; Brasseur yx k'atit). tanatob is not otherwise known; 'caught' follows Brasseur's 'se sont embarrassés dans les branches touffues de l'arbre' (a guess; toggle tanatob'). ca ꜯiquin 'our birds'. xꜭha cut is singular, 'he said' (MS xgha); the speech that follows closes with xeꜭha 'they said'.

sentences.t: “Macu habi chacan chuvi che chiquech, ix catit. Chi cah ta pu ri caꜩ, que be ta cuꜭ, chi be ta qui cazah vloc ri ꜯiquin,” xeꜭha cut.
sentences.l: “Not-then there-is climbing on-top tree to-them, you our-grandmother. Let they-want (ta) also the our-elder-brothers, they go (ta) with-us, let go (ta) they bring-down hither the birds,” they-said then.
sentences.i: “We cannot climb up the tree to them, grandmother. So let our elder brothers be willing (?), let them go with us, and let them go and bring down the birds,” they said.
sentences.n: Macu habi 'there is none, there is no way' (Brasseur ma-cu-habi). chacan 'climb', as in 008 (ch- + acan; toggle chaq'an). chiquech 'to them', the birds (chi + qu- 'their' + ech, as in every earlier part; Brasseur 'pour les prendre'); 'for us' (q- 'our') is also possible with the same letters. caꜩ 'our elder brothers': ca- 'our' + aꜩ 'elder brother' (Brasseur k'atz, c'atz), the plain tz ligature; the toggle gives qatz in the twins' mouths and katz 'their elder brothers' in the narrative. Its partner is chac 'younger brother'. chi cah ta 'let them be willing': chi, the optative, + c- 'they' (qui- before a vowel) + ah 'want' + ta, the xcah 'they wanted' of ¶4 and ¶14 with chi in place of x- (inferred; toggle kaj). Brasseur prints chi cah-ta with plain c (his c = k), where he writes kah for cah 'come down' throughout this passage; his French 'qu'ils y montent' is free. 'Let them come down' (qaj) is the other reading of the letters, but the elder brothers are not up anywhere yet. que be ta cuꜭ 'let them go with us' (MS cug, read ꜭ; toggle quk'). chi be ta qui cazah vloc 'let them go and bring them down': cazah, cah + a causative ending, 'lower, bring down' (Brasseur kazah; toggle qasaj, the modern 'lower'; inferred).

sentences.t: “Vꜩ bala; coh be iuvꜭ zaquiric,” xeꜭha curi caꜩ, ta xe chacouic.
sentences.l: “Good bala; we go with-you dawning,” they-said then-the elder-brothers, then they did-the-overcoming(?).
sentences.i: “Very well; we will go with you at dawn,” said the elder brothers, and with that the twins had won (?).
sentences.n: Vꜩ bala 'very well', the house rendering. coh be 'we go' (c- + oh 'we'). iuvꜭ 'with you' is a doubtful reading: the manuscript has iuvg, four letters at 2× (Brasseur yvuq); printed as written and taken as i- 'your (pl.)' + uꜭ 'company', the u standing for the glide of iv-, as ruꜭ 'with him', cuꜭ 'with them' (toggle iwuk'). zaquiric 'at the dawning' (zac 'white' + -ir + -ic), tomorrow (Brasseur 'demain dès le jour'). caꜩ is now 'their elder brothers' (toggle katz). xe chacouic is taken as chac 'beat, overcome' (009, 010) + -ou- + -ic: -ou- is not a passive ending but the ending of a verb that names the doers, as 008's xchacou 'they did the overcoming' and 006's xbanouic, so 'they were the ones who overcame'. The text does not say who; the twins, whose trick has worked, are supplied in the English (inferred), and the next line names the elder brothers' qui chaquic 'defeat'. A guess (toggle chakowik); Brasseur's French has it as part of the answer ('firent les aînés dans leur réponse').

sentences.t: Xcaminac cut qui naoh qui cabichal chirech qui chaquic Hunbaꜩ, Hunchouen: “Xa ca ꜩolcomih qui ꜭoheic, eu pam;
sentences.l: Was-dead then their thought the-two-of-them toward-it their being-beaten(?) Hunbaꜩ, Hunchouen: “Only we turn-about(?) their being, eu(?) belly;
sentences.i: But the minds of the two of them, Hunbatz and Hunchouen, were dead to their own defeat (?). “We shall only turn about (?) their being, and their bellies (?);
sentences.n: Xcaminac … qui naoh 'their mind was dead': caminac 'dead' (cam + -inac) with x- (as 009's xcaminac). The English follows Brasseur, for whom the wisdom of Hunbatz and Hunchouen 'était morte … relativement à leur défaite'; qui cabichal 'the two of them' could also be the twins, whose plan was settled, and the line is uncertain. chirech 'toward it, concerning'. qui chaquic 'their defeat': chac 'beat' + -ic (toggle chakik). The twins now speak among themselves. ca ꜩolcomih 'we turn about, overturn' (Brasseur 'Nous changerons seulement leur existence'), a guess; toggle by the letters. qui ꜭoheic 'their being'. eu pam is a doubtful reading: the manuscript has eupam at 2×, Brasseur eu pam, his French 'et (la forme de) leur ventre'; eu is left undivided, and may be e u pam 'they, their bellies'. pam 'belly'.

sentences.t: ca ꜩih ta chuxoc rumal nima caxcol mi xqui ban chique. Xoh cam tah, xoh zach tah puch, xcah ri oh qui chac.
sentences.l: our word (ta) let-it-be because great suffering just-now they-did to-us. We die (tah), we are-lost (tah) also, they-wanted the we their younger-brothers.
sentences.i: let our word come to pass, because of the great suffering they have caused us. They wanted us dead, they wanted us lost, we their younger brothers.
sentences.n: ca ꜩih ta chuxoc 'let our word be': chuxoc 'let it be', the creators' word in the first part. nima caxcol 'great suffering', the word of ¶5: what the elder brothers once suffered they put upon the younger. mi xqui ban chique 'they have done to us' (chique 'to us', toggle chiqe). Xoh cam tah, xoh zach tah puch 'that we die, that we be lost', a couplet, xoh 'we' (x- + oh) with tah of wishing. xcah 'they wanted', as in ¶4, where the same xe cam ta clause goes before it (toggle xkaj); Brasseur prints x-kah here, his letters for 'come down', and renders 'qu'il nous arrivât malheur', the misfortune coming down on them; the parallel with ¶4 decides here (inferred). ri oh qui chac 'we, their younger brothers'.

sentences.t: Queheri ala xoh pe vi vloc chi qui ꜭux; quehe cut que ca chac vi; xa retal chi ca bano,” xeꜭha chi quibil quib.
sentences.l: Like youths(?) we came there hither in their heart; thus then them we-beat there; only its-sign (chi) we do-it,” they-said among themselves.
sentences.i: As mere boys (?) we came into their hearts; so now we shall beat them, and do it only as a sign,” they said to each other.
sentences.n: Queheri ala 'like youths': ala 'youth, young man', as in earlier parts; Brasseur has 'Comme des serviteurs, ils nous ont abaissés dans leur pensée', and the sense, mere boys or servants in the elder brothers' eyes, is inferred. xoh pe vi vloc chi qui ꜭux 'we came into their hearts', how they thought of us. que ca chac vi 'we beat them': que is c- + e 'them', ca- 'we', chac 'beat', 009's que ca chac (toggle chak). xa retal 'only a sign': retal, r- + etal 'sign'. chi quibil quib 'among themselves'.

sentences.t: Ta xebe cut chila chuxe che Cante vbi; cachbilan curi caꜩ ta xebec; xqui tiquiba chicut vvbanic.
sentences.l: Then they-went then there at-foot tree Cante its-name; accompanying then-the elder-brothers when they-went; they began again-then blowgunning.
sentences.i: Then they went off to the foot of a tree called Cante, and the elder brothers went along with them; on the way they took up their blowgunning again.
sentences.n: chuxe che 'at the foot of the tree' (chi + v- + xe 'root, base'). Cante is capitalised as the tree's name, as Brasseur prints it. His note: can-te is 'yellow wood' in Tzeltal and Maya, not a K'iche' word, the dyers' wood, and in Maya it can also mean 'snake wood'; kept in the English as a name (toggle Kante). cachbilan 'accompanying (them)': c-, the ongoing, + achbilan 'accompany', the verb of achbil 'companion' (toggle kachb'ilan, as in 006). xqui tiquiba 'they began' (tiquiba 'plant, begin'). vvbanic 'blowgunning', as in ¶8.

sentences.t: Maui ahilan chi ꜯiquin chuvi che que chitihc; xe maihan cut ri caꜩ ta xquil ri ꜯiquin.
sentences.l: Not counted (chi) birds on-top tree they chitihc(?); they marveled then the elder-brothers when they-saw the birds.
sentences.i: There were birds beyond counting in the top of the tree, chirping (?), and the elder brothers marveled when they saw the birds.
sentences.n: maui ahilan 'not counted', beyond number (ahil 'count'). que chitihc is a doubtful reading: the manuscript has chitihc at 2×, with no vowel between h and c, where Brasseur prints chititic and renders 'gazouillaient'; perhaps a slip for chitihic. 'Chirping' is his sense, a guess, and the toggle respells the letters. xe maihan 'they marveled' (Brasseur 's'émerveillaient'; inferred; toggle by the letters). xquil 'they saw'.

sentences.t: “Are curi ꜯiquin, mahabi hun oc xcah vloc chuxe che; ri ca ꜯiquin e maui que cah vloc; xa hix cazah vloc,” xeꜭha cut chire caꜩ.
sentences.l: “This then-the birds, not-there-is one yet came-down hither at-foot tree; the our birds they not they come-down hither; only go-you bring-down hither,” they-said then to-them elder-brothers.
sentences.i: “There are the birds, but not one has yet come down to the foot of the tree; our birds will not come down; just go up and bring them down,” they said to their elder brothers.
sentences.n: mahabi hun oc 'not one yet'. xcah, que cah vloc 'it came down, they come down' (cah 'go down', Brasseur kah; toggle qaj). ri ca ꜯiquin e maui 'our birds, they do not …' (MS rica ꜩi-|quine maui, divided with Brasseur). xa hix cazah vloc is read with Brasseur's xa h'yx: hix 'go, you (pl.)' is written as in 010 (xa hix chi ha 'just go to the house'), the 'go' of he and ho; printed as written. cazah 'bring down', as in ¶12. chire caꜩ 'to their elder brothers'.

sentences.t: “Vꜩ bala,” xeꜭha cut.
sentences.l: “Good bala,” they-said then.
sentences.i: “Very well,” they said.
sentences.n: Vꜩ bala 'very well', the house rendering: the elder brothers agree a second time.

sentences.t: Catepuch xe acanic chuvi che; xnimar cut ri che, xzipoh vpam.
sentences.l: Then-also they climbed on-top tree; it-grew-great then the tree, it-swelled its-belly.
sentences.i: So they climbed up the tree; and the tree grew tall, and its trunk swelled.
sentences.n: xe acanic 'they climbed' (MS xeaca-|nic; Brasseur x-e akanic; toggle aq'anik, as in earlier parts). xnimar 'it grew great': nim 'great' + -ar. xzipoh 'it swelled' (MS z at the line edge, without an ascender; Brasseur x-zipoh; 'swell' is his 'grossit', inferred; toggle xsipoj). vpam 'its belly', the trunk.

sentences.t: Catecut xe rah cah vloc, macu vꜩ chic qui cahic vloc chuvi che Hunbaꜩ, Hunchouen.
sentences.l: Then-then they want come-down hither, not-then good now their coming-down hither on-top tree Hunbaꜩ, Hunchouen.
sentences.i: Then they wanted to come down, but Hunbatz and Hunchouen could no longer get down from the top of the tree.
sentences.n: xe rah 'they wanted to': rah 'want', the form fixed after a plural, as in an earlier part, the wanted act following (cah vloc 'come down'). macu vꜩ chic qui cahic 'their coming down was no longer good', no longer possible: cahic 'coming down' (cah + -ic; toggle qajik).

sentences.t: Xeꜭha cu vloc chuvi che: “Hupacha coh vchanic, ix ca chac? Tocob ca vach! Are ri che ca xibin chic ca quilo, ix ca chac,” xecha vloc chuvi che.
sentences.l: They-said then hither on-top tree: “How we vchanic(?), you our younger-brothers? Pity our face! This the tree it-frightens now we-see-it, you our younger-brothers,” they-said hither on-top tree.
sentences.i: And they called down from the top of the tree: “What has become of us (?), our younger brothers? Pity us! This tree frightens us now to look at, our younger brothers,” they called down from the top of the tree.
sentences.n: The speech is framed by the same words, xeꜭha … vloc chuvi che, xecha vloc chuvi che 'they said down from the top of the tree'; the closing tag has plain ch (xecha), as written, as 013's xcha. Hupacha 'how'. coh vchanic: coh 'we' (c- + oh); vchanic is not otherwise known (Brasseur u chanic, 'Comment ceci nous est-il arrivé'), and the English is a guess along his lines. ix ca chac 'you, our younger brothers' (MS ixcachac). Tocob ca vach 'pity our face' (MS tocob cavach, plain c; Brasseur togob ka vach; toggle toq'ob', as toq'ob' nu wach in an earlier part). ca xibin 'it frightens': xib 'fear' + -in. ca quilo 'we see it'.

sentences.t: Xeꜭha curi Hunahpu, Xbalanque: “Chi quira iuex, chi xima xe i pam; nahlic vꜩam chi hure he chivih; catecut vꜩ i binic,” xe vꜭhax chic cumal qui chac.
sentences.l: They-said then-the Hunahpu, Xbalanque: “Let loosen your-loincloths, let tie-it under your belly; long its-end (chi) pull(?) tail behind-you; then-then good your walking,” they-were-told again by-them their younger-brothers.
sentences.i: Hunahpu and Xbalanque said: “Untie your loincloths and bind them below your bellies, with the ends left long, and pull (?) them out as tails behind you; then you will get about with ease,” the elder brothers were told by their younger brothers.
sentences.n: chi quira iuex 'untie your loincloths': quira 'untie' (modern kir), ex 'loincloth' (Brasseur 'ceintures') with i- 'your (pl.)' and the glide written u, as in iuvꜭ (toggle iwex). chi xima 'tie it': xim 'tie', as in 010. xe i pam 'below your bellies': xe 'root, base' (MS xeipam, divided with Brasseur's xe y pam). nahlic vꜩam 'long its end': nah 'long, far' + -lic (MS na-|hlic); vꜩam 'its point, its tip', the ꜩam 'nose, beak' of the macaw's boast in 004 (toggle utzam). chi hure he chivih is divided with Brasseur's ch'y hure he ch'yvih (MS chihurehe chivih): he is 'tail', as qui he in the next paragraph (modern je'), not the he 'go' of ¶3; hure is not otherwise known, and 'pull' is from Brasseur's 'pendant que vous tirerez par derrière' (a guess); chivih 'behind you'. vꜩ i binic 'your walking will be good' (MS vꜩibinic; Brasseur utz y binic).

sentences.t: “Vve,” xecha cut, ta xqui huruba cut vꜩam qui toc.
sentences.l: “Yes(?),” they-said then, then they-pulled(?) then its-end their loincloth(?).
sentences.i: “Yes,” they said, and they pulled (?) out the ends of their loincloths (?).
sentences.n: Vve stands alone here as the elder brothers' answer, taken as the Ve 'yes' of 006 and 012 written vv (Brasseur Uve, 'C'est fort bien'; inferred); in 009 the same letters vve were taken as ve 'if', and the toggle respells them as there (uwe). xecha with plain ch, as written. xqui huruba 'they pulled' (MS xquihuruba; Brasseur x-qui hurüba, 'en tirant'), taken with hure in the last line (a guess). qui toc 'their girdle, their loincloth' after Brasseur ('leurs ceintures'), not otherwise known (toggle toq, with his k).

sentences.t: Xa pu huzu qui he chi xuxic; xa coy xqui vachibeh chic.
sentences.l: Only also at-once their tail (chi) it-became; only monkey they-took-the-face-of now.
sentences.i: At once these became their tails, and they took on the likeness of monkeys.
sentences.n: huzu 'at once' (toggle jusuk, as in earlier parts). qui he 'their tails' (toggle je'). xuxic 'it became'. xa coy: coy 'monkey' is written with plain c (Brasseur qoy), where the house word is ꜭoy, the monkeys left as the sign of the wooden people in 004; printed as written, the toggle gives k'oy. xqui vachibeh 'they took on the face of': vach 'face' + -ibeh (inferred). The elder brothers join the monkeys of the forest.

sentences.t: Catecut xebe chuvi tac che, chuti huyub, nima huyub; xebec pa tac quichelah, que vohon chic, qui zilah chic chu cab tac che.
sentences.l: Then-then they-went on-top (tac) trees, small mountain, great mountain; they-went into (tac) forests, they vohon(?) now, they swing(?) now on-its arm (tac) trees.
sentences.i: Then they went off over the tops of the trees, over small mountains and great mountains; they went off into the forests, grimacing (?) now, swinging (?) now on the branches of the trees.
sentences.n: The manuscript has chui, a misprint for chuvi, corrected here: Ximénez wrote chui with a raised t-like mark over the i (his heavy accent, as on qui chi in ¶3) and no v, and the text prints chuvi with Brasseur and the nine other chuvi of this part. tac marks things many and scattered: tac che 'trees', tac quichelah 'forests' (toggle k'iche'laj). chuti huyub, nima huyub 'small mountain, great mountain', a couplet for all the land; chuti is a doubtful reading (MS chu + a tall looped letter with an accent + huyub), read t with Brasseur's chuti. huyub is written so here, huiub in ¶2 and ¶4. que vohon, qui zilah are not otherwise known; 'grimacing' and 'swinging' follow Brasseur's 'grimaçant et se balançant sur les branches' (guesses; toggle by the letters; plain z in zilah). chu cab tac che 'on the arms of the trees': cab 'arm, hand' (Brasseur gab; toggle q'ab', as in 012).

sentences.t: Quehe cut qui chacatahic Hunbaꜩ, Hunchouen cumal Hunahpu, Xbalanque; xa rumal qui naual ta xqui bano.
sentences.l: Thus then their being-brought-low Hunbaꜩ, Hunchouen by-them Hunahpu, Xbalanque; only because their spirit-power when they-did-it.
sentences.i: So it was that Hunbatz and Hunchouen were brought low by Hunahpu and Xbalanque; it was only by their spirit power that they did it.
sentences.n: qui chacatahic 'their being brought low', the word used for the downfall of Vucub Caquix and his sons (005–008), and promised for Hunbatz and Hunchouen in 009. qui naual 'their spirit power', the house rendering.

sentences.t: Ta xe opon cut chi cochoch.
sentences.l: Then they arrived-there then at their-home.
sentences.i: Then they came back to their home.
sentences.n: xe opon 'they arrived there'. chi cochoch 'at their home': c- 'their' + ochoch 'home' (toggle kochoch).

sentences.t: Xeꜭha cut, xe oponic ruꜭ catit, ruꜭ pu qui chuch: “Ix catit, naquila mi xqui culvachih ri caꜩ? Xa rax qui vach mi xebec, queheri e chicop chic,” xeꜭha cut.
sentences.l: They-said then, they arrived-there with their-grandmother, with also their mother: “You our-grandmother, what just-now they-met-face-to-face the our-elder-brothers? Only raw(?) their face just-now they-went, like they animals now,” they-said then.
sentences.i: And when they came to their grandmother and their mother, they said: “Grandmother, what has befallen our elder brothers? All at once their faces have gone wild (?), as if they were animals now,” they said.
sentences.n: ruꜭ catit, ruꜭ pu qui chuch 'to their grandmother and to their mother' (MS rug, read ꜭ): catit is here c- 'their' + atit (toggle katit), and in the speech Ix catit 'our grandmother' (toggle qatit); qui chuch is Xquic. The twins speak as if they knew nothing. naquila 'what'. xqui culvachih 'they met face to face' (cul 'meet' + vach 'face' + -ih). Xa rax qui vach: rax 'green, raw, fresh' (rax camic 'sudden death' in 009); 'gone wild' is a guess, and Brasseur takes it as 'en un instant'. chicop 'animal' (Brasseur's note in 013: also a brute, a savage).

sentences.t: “Ve naquila mi xiban chique ivaꜩ, mi xin icalaba, mi pu xin ichiquiba.
sentences.l: “If what just-now you-did to-them your-elder-brothers, just-now me you-calaba(?), just-now also me you-chiquiba(?).
sentences.i: “If it is you who have done this to your elder brothers, you have ruined me (?), you have cast me down (?).
sentences.n: Ve 'if'. mi xiban 'you (pl.) have done' (MS mixiban, i- joined). ivaꜩ 'your elder brothers': iv- 'your (pl.)' + aꜩ (toggle iwatz). mi xin icalaba, mi pu xin ichiquiba is a couplet: x- + in 'me' + i- 'you (pl.)' + the verb (MS mixinicalaba, xinichiquiba; Brasseur mi-x-in y galaba). calaba is 013's xe a calaba, 'laid waste' there; here 'ruined' after Brasseur's 'vous m'avez ruinée'. chiquiba follows his 'abîmée de tristesse'. Both are guesses, and the toggle respells the letters.

sentences.t: Mata quehe xiban chique ivaꜩ, ix vi,” xꜭha ri atit chiquech Hunahpu, Xbalanque.
sentences.l: Do-not thus you-did to-them your-elder-brothers, you (vi),” she-said the grandmother to-them Hunahpu, Xbalanque.
sentences.i: Do not do such things to your elder brothers, you two,” the grandmother said to Hunahpu and Xbalanque.
sentences.n: Mata 'do not': ma 'not' + ta. xiban 'you (pl.) did' carries the sense of a prohibition here (inferred). ix vi 'you, you there' (Brasseur 'ó mes enfants'); 'you two' gives the plural. xꜭha, singular, closes the old woman's speech.

sentences.t: Xeꜭha chicut chire catit: “Mi xbizonic, ix catit; xchivil chic qui vach ri caꜩ; xque vlic.
sentences.l: They-said again-then to-her their-grandmother: “Do-not you(?)-grieve, you our-grandmother; you-shall-see again their face the our-elder-brothers; they-shall come-here.
sentences.i: Then they said to their grandmother: “Do not grieve, grandmother; you will see our elder brothers' faces again; they will come back.
sentences.n: Mi xbizonic 'do not grieve', as in 010, Brasseur's sense. Brasseur divides M'yx bizonic, mi + ix 'you (pl.)', which would make the x the ix of the plural 'you' run into mi (inferred; the same with mi xꜩeenic in the next line); the form is not otherwise clear. Over catit the manuscript has a small raised k, not printed. xchivil 'you (pl.) shall see': xch- (xchi- before a vowel) + iv- 'you (pl.)' + il 'see' (Brasseur x-ch'yvil), the plural of respect. xque vlic 'they shall come': xque taken as the future x- + que 'they' (inferred; MS xquevlic; Brasseur x-que ulic, 'ils retourneront').

sentences.t: Xere chicut vtihouic va chive, ix catit; taqui mi xꜩeenic. Cahhana qui ꜫih,” xeꜭha cut.
sentences.l: So again-then its-testing this to-you, you our-grandmother; take-care(?) do-not you-laugh. Cahhana(?) their day,” they-said then.
sentences.i: But this will be a test for you, grandmother: take care (?) not to laugh. Now try their fortune (?),” they said.
sentences.n: vtihouic 'its testing': v- + tih 'try, test' (the tihobal 'trial' of 010) + -ou + -ic (toggle utijowik). va chive 'this, for you'. taqui is not otherwise known; 'take care' is Brasseur's 'prenez garde' (a guess; toggle taki). mi xꜩeenic 'do not laugh': ꜩeen 'laugh', ꜩe 'laughter' + -n, + -ic; the x is taken, with Brasseur's m'yx-tzeenic, as ix 'you (pl.)' (inferred, as Mi xbizonic above; toggle xtze'nik). Cahhana qui ꜫih is a doubtful reading: the manuscript has cahhana at 2×, with two h, printed as written and undivided; Brasseur prints C'a na qui gih and renders 'Éprouvez maintenant leur fortune', and the English is a guess along his lines (toggle Kajjana by the letters). qui ꜫih 'their day', perhaps 'their lot' (MS quiquih, the q-shaped letter + u read ꜫ with Brasseur's gih).

sentences.t: Catepuch xqui tiquiba zuanic, Hunahpu Coy xqui zuah.
sentences.l: Then-also they began fluting, Hunahpu Coy they-fluted-it.
sentences.i: Then they began to play the flute: they played the tune Hunahpu Coy.
sentences.n: zuanic, zuah 'fluting, play on the flute': zu 'flute' made a verb (Brasseur's note: zuah, zuanic, 'jouer, toucher d'un instrument, en particulier un instrument à vent, comme la flûte; le radical est zu'; toggle suanik, suaj). Hunahpu Coy 'Hunahpu Monkey', the name of the tune: the manuscript has hunahpu, then a struck letter (a crossed z- or 4-like stroke), then coy; the struck letter is not printed, as at the end of 013. It may be a cuatrillo that Ximénez replaced, or the cuatrillo written as a 4 beside the c; doubtful. coy has plain c, as xa coy in ¶20, where the house word is ꜭoy; the toggle gives K'oy. Brasseur's note: the Hunahpu-Qoy, 'singe de Hunahpu', is a dance still performed by the Indians of Guatemala at certain feasts, with wooden masks, costumes and music of its own. The part ends at Ximénez's paragraph break; the grandmother's test follows.

about: Xquic gives birth to Hunahpu and Xbalanque on the mountain, and the grandmother is not there to see it. Brought into the house, the babies will not sleep, and the old woman has them thrown out: they are laid on an anthill, then on thorns, where Hunbatz and Hunchouen, out of envy, want them to die. The elder brothers will not take them into the house, and the twins grow up on the mountain. Hunbatz and Hunchouen are great flute players and singers, painters and carvers, sages who know from the first what their younger brothers are, but envy blinds them. The twins hunt with the blowgun every day; no one loves them, they are fed only after the others have eaten, and Hunbatz and Hunchouen eat the birds they bring; still they take no offence. One day they come home without birds: the birds are caught up in a tree, they say, so let our elder brothers come and bring them down. At the foot of a tree called Cante the elder brothers climb up; the tree grows and swells, and they cannot get down. The twins tell them to untie their loincloths, bind them under their bellies and pull the long ends out behind; the ends become tails, the elder brothers become monkeys, and they go off over the treetops into the forest. The twins go home and tell their grandmother, who grieves; they promise she will see her grandsons' faces again, but it will be a test for her, and she must not laugh. Then they begin to play the tune Hunahpu Coy.
